# Implementation status

The supervisor already provides deployment loading/version pinning, per-invocation process supervision, and runtime-budget enforcement inside the BEAM guest.

The in-guest tree has a minimal stable `bmscl_sup` above the replaceable
`bmscl_runtime_sup`. The trusted `bmscl_runtime` API drains/stops/restarts that
subtree while preserving the outer PID; timeout preserves the existing runtime.
Replacements start empty and require explicit verified artifact reactivation.
See `runtime-replacement.md`. Release installation, zero-downtime shard handoff,
and durable desired-state replay are not implemented by this API.

Current platform boundary:

```text
API placement -> Firecracker runtime host -> tenant microVM ready
                                           X
                                      guest dispatch
                                           X
                                  bmscl-supervisor
```

The missing `X` is the trusted runtime-host invocation bridge documented in `runtime-host-bridge.md`. Until it exists, control-plane `runtime_ready` must not be reported as successful Hosted Gleam handler execution.

# Customer-signed builds and BeamScale admission receipts

BeamScale does not need to rebuild customer applications on BeamScale infrastructure.

The trust boundary is deliberately split:

1. The customer builds with `bmscl-compiler`, packages the exact BEAM tree, and signs the artifact with a customer-controlled Ed25519 key.
2. The BeamScale control plane resolves that key from the customer's registered key set, verifies the signature and exact digests, then runs the cheap `bmscl-compiler verify` admission path over the finished BEAM files. This path does not invoke Gleam, download dependencies, or rebuild.
3. Successful shared-tier admission produces `admission-receipt.json`, signed by a BeamScale admission key.
4. The tenant runtime/P1/P2 verifies the BeamScale admission receipt plus the exact manifest, admission report, provenance and BEAM-tree digest before loading worker modules.

A customer signature proves authorization and byte provenance. It is never the production runtime safety root. A malicious customer can sign arbitrary bytes, so shared-tier safety still requires BeamScale's independent verify-only admission.

Production runtime defaults are fail closed:

```erlang
{require_admission_receipt, true},
{trusted_admission_keys, []},
{require_attestation, false},
{require_trusted_build_provenance, false}
```

`trusted_admission_keys` must be provisioned by trusted runtime configuration. Customer public keys stay in the control plane and do not need to be distributed to every tenant microVM.

The receipt binds the customer key id, build/source hashes, exact manifest/admission/provenance hashes, policy hash, compiler version/revision and verifier version. Runtime activation therefore costs hashing plus Ed25519 verification rather than a rebuild or full source re-analysis.

# BeamScale Durable Actors

BeamScale Durable Actors are the stateful service tier for workloads that need
stable identity, serialized state transitions, durable state, hibernation, and
location-aware execution. The product abstraction is similar to a Durable
Object, but the runtime is Erlang/OTP-native.

Tracking:
- Epic: https://github.com/beamscale/bmscl-supervisor/issues/72
- Runtime V1: https://github.com/beamscale/bmscl-supervisor/issues/73

## Logical identity is not a PID

The stable identity of a logical actor is:

```text
{tenant_id, application_id, namespace, object_key}
```

PIDs, BEAM nodes, actor buckets, and host machines are implementation details.
A logical actor may be restored on a different physical actor without changing
its public identity.

## Virtual shards and tenant-only multiplexing

The runtime maps a logical identity to a deterministic virtual shard, then maps
that shard into an actor bucket.

```text
logical object
    -> virtual shard
    -> actor bucket
    -> physical Erlang actor
```

A physical Erlang actor may own many virtual shards, but every shard on that
actor MUST belong to the same tenant. No physical durable actor may multiplex
objects from different tenants.

This permits cold tenants to use very few BEAM processes while allowing hot
shards to be split onto additional same-tenant actors later.

## Serialization

The logical object is the serialization boundary.

The target semantic is one active state-changing turn per logical object, not
one globally active turn for every shard multiplexed by the physical actor.
Early implementations may serialize more aggressively, but the public contract
must not depend on that physical scheduling choice.

## Durable state

The actor is the execution/serialization authority. The storage backend is the
durability and stale-owner authority.

Persisted state is an **opaque binary payload**, not an arbitrary Erlang term.
Trusted runtime codecs own encoding/versioning. VM-local values such as PIDs,
refs, funs, and ports must never enter the durable format.

The initial storage contract is defined by `bmscl_durable_store`:

```text
load(logical_identity)
claim_owner(virtual_shard_scope) -> authoritative epoch
commit(logical_identity, expected_version, virtual_shard_scope, owner_epoch, state)
```

Logical object identity deliberately excludes the virtual shard. Placement may
change without changing the object's durable key. Fencing, however, is scoped
to the virtual shard because that is the minimum independently movable
ownership unit in V1.

A successful mutation response must not be returned until the corresponding
state transition has durably committed.

Postgres or CockroachDB are suitable first backends. A colocated replicated
store can be introduced later without changing the logical actor API.

## Fencing epochs

The current local registry sequence/epoch is useful for the prototype but is
NOT a distributed fencing token across registry or node restarts.

Production multi-node ownership requires a monotonic authoritative epoch that
is allocated by the durable ownership store, not chosen by the caller. Storage
must reject stale owners even when the stale owner still has a live process and
even when the new owner has not loaded or changed the particular object yet.

That last condition is why fencing is checked against a shard-level ownership
record rather than an epoch copied only into each object's row.

Example:

```text
node A owns epoch 46
network partition
node B is assigned epoch 47
node A tries to commit with 46 -> reject
node B commits with 47 -> accept
```

Never infer safety from "the old owner probably died".

## Lifecycle

Expected logical-object lifecycle:

```text
cold
 -> restoring
 -> active
 -> draining
 -> hibernated / evicted
 -> restoring
```

Objects should load lazily. Idle objects may be removed from RAM after durable
state has been committed. Entire tenant actor buckets may also disappear when
idle and be recreated on demand.

## Deployment generation

Durable actors must remain pinned to an admitted deployment generation while a
turn is executing. The runtime must fail closed rather than silently reuse an
actor pinned to a different deployment generation. Migration to a new code
generation is a separate controlled operation and must not silently change code
halfway through a turn.

The admitted artifact must also bind the durable namespace and shard layout.
Routes are not allowed to point a Durable Actor execution class at an ordinary
lambda artifact or at an artifact admitted with a different namespace/layout.

## Alarms

Durable alarms are persisted metadata, not only `send_after` timers.
A live actor may use a local timer as an optimization, but restart recovery must
scan/recover due alarms from durable state. Delivery should be treated as
at-least-once.

## External side effects

BeamScale should not claim exactly-once external effects. A crash can happen
between an external side effect and the durable state commit.

Use request IDs, idempotency keys, and a transactional outbox pattern for
external effects.

## Placement and migration

V1 can use a single home region. Distributed migration follows:

```text
stop admitting new turns
 -> drain in-flight work
 -> commit/checkpoint
 -> advance owner epoch
 -> assign destination
 -> restore
 -> update routing
```

After the epoch advances, the source must be unable to commit.

## Adaptive splitting

Shard layout is deliberately independent from logical actor identity.

A cold tenant may initially map many virtual shards onto one actor. When one
shard becomes hot, placement can move that shard to a different same-tenant
actor. An extremely hot object may eventually occupy an actor bucket by itself.

Useful split signals include:
- mailbox latency,
- reductions/CPU,
- heap/memory,
- active object count,
- request rate,
- commit latency.

## Security boundary

An Erlang process is not the hostile-tenant boundary.

Durable Actors remain inside the same BeamScale defense-in-depth model:
compiler admission, capability-only SDK surface, trusted runtime bridges, and
the OS/BEAM sandbox. Tenant code must not receive raw code-loading, filesystem,
process creation, NIF, BEAM distribution, arbitrary socket, or host-control
authority.

## Delivery phases

1. Contract + single-node semantics.
2. Postgres/Cockroach persistence, lazy restore, hibernation, alarms.
3. Distributed placement, monotonic epochs, failover.
4. Adaptive shard splitting.
5. Regional migration and websocket hibernation.

See the parent epic and linked child issues for implementation ownership.

# Durable Queue quorum log V1

Tracking: #102, #103

This document defines the first BeamScale Durable Queue storage/replication
contract. It is intentionally narrower than a complete Raft implementation.
Leader election, replica transport, fsync-backed segment IO, and dynamic
consensus-group membership remain separate layers. This contract defines the
invariants those layers must preserve.

## Record framing

Every queue record has deterministic binary framing:

```text
magic                4 bytes  BMSQ
version              u8       1
flags                u8       0
term                 u64
sequence             u64
timestamp_unix_ms    u64
idempotency_key_len  u32
payload_len          u32
idempotency_key      bytes
payload              bytes
checksum             32 bytes SHA-256(all preceding bytes)
```

`term` and `sequence` are capped at JavaScript's maximum safe integer so the
same authority values can cross JSON/JS tooling without silent rounding.

The frame checksum covers both metadata and payload. A copied individual record
therefore remains independently verifiable during repair and range transfer.

## Immutable segments

`bmscl_queue_segment` packages contiguous verified frames into an immutable V1
segment:

```text
magic           4 bytes  BMSG
version         u8       1
flags           u8       0
base_sequence   u64
record_count    u32
body_bytes      u64
body            repeated {frame_len:u32, frame:bytes}
digest          32 bytes SHA-256(header + body)
```

A segment is rejected unless:

- the outer digest matches;
- every inner queue frame checksum matches;
- every frame boundary is exact; and
- record sequences are contiguous from `base_sequence`.

The manifest records base/last sequence, record count, total bytes, digest, and
minimum/maximum term. Segment files are immutable once sealed. A future disk
writer owns fsync/rename semantics; this module defines the deterministic bytes
that writer must persist.

The double integrity layer is intentional:

```text
segment digest
    protects manifest/header + frame boundaries + complete segment bytes

record checksum
    protects one independently copied/repaired queue record
```

## Partition state

The V1 quorum tracker maintains:

```text
partition_id
term
leader
replicas
quorum
next_sequence
last_sequence
committed_sequence
entries[index]
durable_progress[replica]
idempotency[key]
```

`durable_progress` means the replica has durably accepted every record through
that sequence. It is not merely a network receive watermark.

## Producer acknowledgement

A leader append first becomes locally durable and receives a sequence. The
producer must not treat `pending` as success.

```text
append on leader
  -> local durable sequence N
  -> replicate
  -> quorum durable progress >= N
  -> committed_sequence advances to N
  -> producer may be acknowledged
```

The state machine advances the committed prefix from the quorum match index only
when the candidate contains an entry from the current term. Committing that
current-term entry commits the earlier prefix as well. A quorum that happens to
contain only retained old-term entries does not independently advance commit in
the new term. This mirrors the safety rule used by Raft without claiming that
V1 implements Raft election/transport.

## Ambiguous producer outcomes

### Leader dies before quorum

The record is uncommitted. A newly elected term may truncate it. A producer can
retry its idempotency key and receive a new append if the original record was
not retained.

### Leader dies after quorum but before reply

The record is part of the committed prefix and cannot be truncated. Its
idempotency key survives recovery. Retrying the same key resolves to the
original sequence rather than creating another logical append.

This provides deterministic retry semantics without claiming exactly-once
external effects.

## Term changes and fencing

A term change is accepted only when:

- the term strictly increases;
- the selected leader belongs to the replica set;
- the retained last sequence is at least the committed sequence; and
- the retained last sequence does not exceed the known tail.

The new term deterministically deletes entries after the retained sequence.
That suffix was never committed. The committed prefix is never legal to
truncate.

Old leaders cannot append under their old term. A process may remain alive, but
its term no longer grants authority.

The queue term and the shared Durable Actor/shard `ownership_epoch` are related
but distinct:

```text
placement / ownership epoch
    controls which physical shard owner may act

queue term
    controls which queue-replication leader may append in that replica group

sequence / committed_sequence
    controls the ordered queue history
```

Do not overload one of these numbers to mean all three things.

## Bounded backpressure

Each partition has `max_uncommitted`. When replication stalls and the difference
between `last_sequence` and `committed_sequence` reaches that bound, the leader
rejects new appends with `queue_replication_backpressure` rather than allowing
RAM/mailbox usage to grow without bound.

This is an admission boundary, not the final disk-quota policy.

## Replay boundary

Replay exposes only `1..committed_sequence`. Locally appended but uncommitted
records must never become visible to queue consumers.

Future retention will move the earliest replayable sequence forward after
consumer/replay constraints allow whole immutable segments to be deleted.

## Shard migration

The shared shard-handoff barrier is bound to:

```text
barrier_position = committed_sequence
```

Never use `last_sequence` for queue migration. The uncommitted suffix may be
truncated after a leader change and therefore is not durable queue truth.

There is a second subtle rule: quorum commit does **not** mean every surviving
replica has reached the barrier. For example:

```text
replicas = A / B / C
quorum   = 2

sequence 10_003 is durable on A and B
C is only durable through 9_991

committed_sequence = 10_003
```

If placement changes from A/B/C to B/C/D, the initial handoff progress must be:

```text
B = 10_003
C = 9_991
D = 0
```

It is unsafe to initialize C at 10_003 merely because C belonged to the old
replica set. `bmscl_queue_rebalance` therefore seeds the shared handoff state
from the quorum log's actual `durable_progress` map. Both C and D must report
catch-up through 10_003 before placement cutover may fence A.

An uncommitted tail remains outside the barrier:

```text
last_sequence      = 10_005
committed_sequence = 10_003
```

Entries 10_004 and 10_005 require normal queue-term recovery and may be retained
or truncated depending on the authoritative leader history.

## Next implementation layers

1. fsync-backed segment writer with atomic seal/rename and manifest inventory;
2. follower range/segment transfer;
3. disk-backed recovery that reconstructs the committed prefix;
4. consensus/election transport using this state machine's term/index rules;
5. replica quarantine and repair for checksum corruption;
6. segment retention tied to consumer-group/replay watermarks;
7. multiplexed replica groups for cold partitions and explicit hot-partition
   graduation using the shared shard handoff protocol.

# Dynamic HTTP routing

The production router is a P2/daddy responsibility. P1/granddaddy remains route-agnostic and long-lived.

Route source directories are build-time input only. Deploy activates an immutable route snapshot that maps method/path to logical `function_id`, immutable `deployment_id`, artifact digest, and BEAM entrypoint. The request path is never converted to a filesystem path at runtime.

For BeamScale, activation verifies the artifact first, then maps the target to a bounded `(function_slot, generation_slot)` namespace before it is published. New requests pin the selected deployment generation. Existing root/affine invocations keep their generation until they drain.

Route snapshot replacement is atomic. Adding or deleting a source route changes the next snapshot and does not require replacing P1 or restarting the BEAM VM. P2 runtime/middleware code may be replaced separately from route data.

The route manifest authority is `ores.routes.v1` emitted by the build/deploy tooling. `source_path` is provenance for change detection and debugging only.

# Dynamic routing, cache invalidation, and hot code

BeamScale splits the long-lived tenant runtime into two supervision layers:

```text
bmscl_sup                         # granddaddy: stable bootstrap only
  -> bmscl_runtime_sup            # daddy: replaceable runtime subtree
       -> bmscl_deployment_manager
       -> bmscl_budget_manager
       -> bmscl_route_table
       -> bmscl_route_refresh
       -> bmscl_invocation_sup
       -> bmscl_guest_control
```

The granddaddy must not parse HTTP routes, own Wisp routing tables, evaluate middleware, perform network I/O, or depend on Redis availability. Its job is to keep the replaceable runtime subtree alive and provide a stable lifecycle boundary. The daddy is also a pure OTP supervisor: mutable routing and control-plane work belongs in supervised workers beneath it.

## Route identity and request dispatch

A Lambda/actor is identified by repository-relative source path. The build/deploy pipeline derives route metadata from that path and publishes a complete desired route snapshot. A route target is conceptually:

```erlang
#{
  deployment_id => <<"content-addressed-generation-id">>,
  actor_path => <<"routes/get/users/[id]">>,
  entrypoint => <<"worker:handle/2">>
}.
```

The route key is the normalized `{Method, Path}` pair, for example `{<<"GET">>, <<"/users/:id">>}`. `ANY` is the fallback method for a path when an exact method entry is absent.

`bmscl_route_table` owns the in-memory versioned snapshot. Installing a new snapshot is atomic with respect to generation holds: every referenced deployment generation is pinned before the table becomes visible, and holds for generations no longer referenced are released only after the replacement succeeds. That prevents normal deployment GC from purging code that a published route still references.

`bmscl_http_router` is the HTTP-facing resolution boundary. It resolves through `bmscl_route_table`, then invokes the exact `deployment_id` through `bmscl_router`. The invocation path takes its own per-request pin, so an in-flight request remains generation-affine even if the route snapshot changes immediately afterward.

## Route refresh and Redis/cache model

Redis or another shared control-plane store is useful as a snapshot cache and invalidation bus, but it is not the execution authority.

Recommended logical keys/channels are:

```text
bmscl:{tenant}:{env}:routes:version       -> monotonic integer
bmscl:{tenant}:{env}:routes:snapshot      -> signed canonical route snapshot
bmscl:{tenant}:{env}:routes:updated       -> pub/sub notification containing version + digest

bmscl:{tenant}:{env}:middleware:{digest}  -> optional immutable metadata/artifact cache
bmscl:{tenant}:{env}:middleware:updated   -> pub/sub invalidation notification
```

For larger BEAM bundles, keep immutable bytes in object/artifact storage and put only digest, signature, size, and object location in Redis. Redis can still cache hot bundles opportunistically.

`bmscl_route_refresh` is a child of `bmscl_runtime_sup`. A pub/sub notification is only a wake-up hint. On startup, reconnect, notification, and periodic reconciliation, the refresh worker should fetch the authoritative version/snapshot through its route-source adapter and reconcile the complete snapshot into `bmscl_route_table`. A dropped pub/sub message therefore cannot permanently leave the process on stale routing state.

The source adapter is responsible for control-plane transport and verification policy. Before a snapshot is admitted it should verify the expected schema plus canonical digest/signature and ensure all referenced deployment or middleware generations are available. Runtime workers should never treat an unverified pub/sub payload as executable route truth.

The granddaddy may be notified indirectly through normal OTP supervision if the replaceable runtime subtree becomes unhealthy. There is intentionally no Redis client or route parser in `bmscl_sup`.

## Adding, changing, and deleting route folders

For deployed Git commit `A` and candidate commit `B`, the build/deploy pipeline compares route/Lambda roots rather than rebuilding every Lambda indiscriminately:

- **new route folder:** build and sign only that Lambda; add its target to the desired snapshot;
- **changed route folder:** rebuild/sign only that Lambda; replace its deployment generation in the desired snapshot;
- **deleted route folder:** upload no new artifact; omit it from the complete snapshot and remove/tombstone the control-plane target;
- **unchanged route folder:** retain its existing deployment generation and snapshot entry without upload or reload.

A complete snapshot makes deletion deterministic. Runtime reconciliation never has to guess whether absence from a fragile incremental pub/sub message means "unchanged" or "deleted". Delta operations may be supported locally, but the recoverable control-plane contract remains a monotonic complete snapshot.

## Middleware hot loading

Do not evaluate Erlang or Gleam source fetched from Redis inside the production host runtime. Use the same admission pipeline as Lambda code:

```text
Gleam/Erlang source
  -> pinned compiler
  -> policy/admission checks
  -> deterministic BEAM bundle
  -> content digest
  -> build-service signature
  -> immutable artifact store/cache
  -> verified BEAM load
  -> atomic route/middleware snapshot swap
```

Prepare and verify every module before publishing references to the new generation. Existing requests stay pinned to the old generation; fresh requests resolve the new snapshot.

Trusted platform middleware should use versioned/content-addressed module namespaces so old and new generations can coexist while requests drain. Tenant-authored middleware should preferably be compiled into the tenant actor artifact, or execute through the same restricted guest/capability boundary, rather than gaining host-runtime authority.

## Wisp / HTTP adapter boundary

Wisp or another Gleam/Erlang HTTP adapter belongs beneath the daddy and should remain thin:

```text
socket -> parse request -> bmscl_http_router.resolve(method, path)
       -> exact deployment generation -> fresh actor -> response
```

The HTTP adapter does not own route truth. `bmscl_route_table` owns the hot snapshot, `bmscl_route_refresh` owns reconciliation, `bmscl_deployment_manager` owns deployment generations and pins, and `bmscl_invocation_sup` owns fresh request actors. Keeping those boundaries separate lets routing state, control-plane connectivity, actor generations, and the HTTP server lifecycle evolve independently without making the granddaddy complex.

## Operational invariants

1. `bmscl_sup` stays small and stable for months; route or middleware churn must not require replacing it.
2. `bmscl_runtime_sup` may be replaced as a unit when daddy-level logic changes, while ordinary Lambda deployments hot-swap generations beneath it.
3. Every published route refers to an exact deployment generation, never merely "latest".
4. A route generation is held for the lifetime of the snapshot reference and separately pinned for each admitted request.
5. Fresh requests observe the current atomic route snapshot; in-flight requests finish on the generation they started with.
6. Pub/sub is invalidation only; authoritative snapshot refetch makes recovery deterministic after missed messages or reconnects.
7. Folder-level build/deploy diffing avoids redeploying unchanged Lambdas for a whole-repository commit.

# Execution security classes

BeamScale has one FaaS control plane but more than one execution-security class.

## Standard FaaS: dense bare-process runtime

The default short-lived FaaS path is optimized for very high density and low
cost. It runs on the shared host fleet and keeps tenant authority deliberately
small.

Tenant code does not receive ambient authority to:

- spawn arbitrary BEAM processes
- spawn OS processes or open ports
- read or write the host filesystem
- load native code/NIFs
- open arbitrary network connections

Those operations remain behind BeamScale capability brokers and the hosted ABI.
The host/runtime may use the filesystem and OS on behalf of the tenant; that
does not make those facilities directly available to tenant code.

## Phoenix v1: Firecracker microVM

Phoenix applications need a substantially broader BEAM runtime surface:
supervision trees, DynamicSupervisor, Registry, PubSub, WebSocket/LiveView
processes, timers, and other normal OTP behavior. `phoenix_v1` therefore
requires the Firecracker execution backend.

The initial Phoenix authority profile is:

- one tenant per microVM
- BEAM process spawning allowed inside the guest
- release filesystem mounted read-only
- quota-limited writable `/tmp`
- persistent storage only through an explicit capability
- network access capability-scoped
- OS process spawning/ports denied by default
- NIF/native-code loading denied by default

A future product option may intentionally grant OS-process or native-code
capabilities, but neither follows merely from selecting Phoenix.

## Durable actor v1: Firecracker microVM

Durable Actors also require the Firecracker backend. The VM is initially
single-tenant, while logical Durable Objects are multiplexed into tenant-only
Erlang actor buckets.

Durable user turns remain serialized. BEAM process creation is
platform-managed rather than an unrestricted user capability so background
processes cannot silently violate the single-turn object model.

Filesystem and OS-process rules match the conservative Firecracker baseline:
read-only release, quota-limited temporary storage, capability-backed
persistence, and no ambient OS process spawning or native code.

## Fail-closed backend admission

`bmscl_execution_boundary` derives placement from the normalized route and
refuses an experimental Phoenix/Durable profile that claims `bare_process`.

`bmscl_experimental_runtime` independently verifies that a target is
Firecracker-class before invoking an external dispatcher. A bare-process target
cannot enter the Firecracker dispatcher through that API.

Firecracker worker implementations should call
`bmscl_execution_policy:admit_worker/2` when accepting work. This provides a
second admission point at the destination and prevents a Firecracker-only
profile from executing in a bare-process worker pool.

The route layer also applies the experimental-profile feature gate before
dispatching request, connection, or durable-actor operations.

## Signed host-to-worker contract

Firecracker placement is backed by the short-lived, tenant-bound signed
dispatch protocol documented in [MicroVM runtime contract v1](microvm-runtime-contract.md).
The signing key remains outside the guest; the trusted launcher verifies the
ticket before creating or reusing a single-tenant VM.
